claims.text: Adding a low concentration of Ru or Sn to Pt can form a Pt-based single-atom alloy with isolated secondary-metal atoms adjacent to Pt sites.
Secondary-metal atoms modify the local coordination environment of Pt sites.
Proximity to the secondary-metal atoms shifts the Pt d-band center.
The shift in the Pt d-band center decreases the binding energy of poisoning intermediates.
CO and CHx species are poisoning intermediates during ethanol oxidation on Pt.
Weaker binding facilitates removal of CO and CHx species from the catalyst surface.
Easier removal of poisoning intermediates enhances ethanol dehydrogenation and C–C bond cleavage.
Enhanced dehydrogenation and C–C bond cleavage promote complete 12-electron oxidation of ethanol to CO2.
Atomic-scale alloying with Ru or Sn will increase ethanol-oxidation current density relative to pure Pt nanoparticles.
Atomic-scale alloying with Ru or Sn will increase selectivity toward CO2 relative to pure Pt nanoparticles.
In situ spectroscopy will reveal shifts in Pt binding energies in the single-atom alloys.
In situ FTIR will show reduced accumulation of poisoning intermediates on the single-atom alloys.
The secondary metal will remain atomically dispersed during durability testing.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the secondary metal remains stably atomically dispersed in the Pt matrix.
Loss of atomic dispersion under harsh or prolonged cycling may cause catalytic behavior to revert toward that of pure Pt.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that the mechanism is expected to fail when atomic dispersion is lost, whereas the falsification rule treats failure to retain atomic dispersion as falsification of the mechanism itself. Loss of the proposed active structure would not decisively test the mechanism under the stated applicability condition.
